# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 AI’s impact on the workforce: “Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition hours after release of the draft text.

 Frontier AI Government (Title I)

 Workforce (Title II)

 Cybersecurity (Title III)

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV)

 Transparency in frontier AI models 

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (Section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (Section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (Section 113).

 Section 111 

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a “frontier AI framework” focused on risk mitigation and the handling of “catastrophic risk.” All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any “critical safety incidents” to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

 Section 112 

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee “independent verification organizations (IVOs)” that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform “audits and assessments.”

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s “frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks.”

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113 

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

 All three sections borrow heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER

 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

> **INTERNAL DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off, Fri 23 Oct 2026.** Do not transmit from this workspace. Delete this note block and fill every [BRACKETED] item before sending. October 23, 2026

United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We write to respond to your invitation for comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft.

Our bottom line is simple, and we want to state it plainly at the top: **we oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium** — a pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP (a standard measure of the computing power used to train a model) until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.

We say this after reading the draft, and after two years of hearing from our members. Parents ask us who is accountable if a frontier model is stolen. Warehouse and hospital workers ask what happens to the systems that increasingly schedule them. Our researchers cannot point us to a single developer who can demonstrate control of its most capable system. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

We are grateful that you released this as a discussion draft and invited feedback before introduction. That process is why we are engaging rather than merely objecting. Our comments follow.

## 1. The draft measures the race; it does not slow it

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of the model weights of a frontier model; a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and loss of control of a model. Those are exactly the events that no reporting regime can undo. Once weights are out, they are out.

Section 111 responds to that reality with disclosure. Large frontier developers must publish a "frontier AI framework" describing how they assess and manage catastrophic risk. All frontier developers must publish transparency reports before or alongside deployment, and must report critical safety incidents to the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) — within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours for imminent catastrophic risk.

Section 112 responds with an audit. Large frontier developers must retain a CAISI-licensed Independent Verification Organization to verify compliance and assess the adequacy of their frameworks, semi-annually and on request.

We support transparency. We support audits. But read together, these are the parts of a safety regime that operate *after* the hardest decisions have already been made. No provision in the draft asks anyone to stop, and no official in the draft has the power to make them. An IVO can refer a violation to the Attorney General, and must refer matters involving imminent catastrophic risk — but referral is not suspension, and an audit delivered six months into a deployment is not a gate. The principal sanction, civil penalties of up to $1 million per day, prices non-compliance for companies spending billions on training runs.

There is also the sunset. Sections 111 and 112 expire after three years unless Congress reauthorizes them. A safety regime that expires on a schedule is a pilot program, not a floor.

## 2. The thresholds in Section 101 pick a perimeter that decays

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, and tiers developers by revenue ($50 million for a "frontier developer," $500 million for a "large frontier developer").

We agree that 10^26 is the right line. It is the same line our moratorium proposal uses. But as a regulatory perimeter it decays quickly. Training compute for frontier language models has grown roughly five-fold per year since 2020. The first model estimated to cross 10^26 FLOP was Grok-3, released in February 2025; on current trend, around 30 notable models will sit above that threshold by the start of 2027, and over 200 by 2030 (Epoch AI, Feb. 2026). What is "frontier" in this draft will be unremarkable by 2028, and the bill's obligations will follow the frontier upward rather than holding it.

The revenue tiers leave out actors our members worry about most: labs under the revenue line, non-profit and university efforts, and foreign or state-backed developers whose models matter regardless of what they earn. And the definition of catastrophic risk — death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage — is pegged to identifiable catastrophes. Our members worry as much about slow, cumulative harms: gradual loss of human oversight, misuse that never crosses the 50-person line, and models that quietly become harder to inspect. Those harms fall outside the draft's frame entirely.

## 3. Section 121 would disarm the states. We oppose it.

Section 121 preempts state law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years, and "development" reaches every act a developer performs or directs before deployment. Your own FAQ concedes that California's AB 2013 and part of SB 942 would be preempted, and that the frontier safety laws — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's SB 315 — would be "federalized."

Consider what that means in practice. SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Section 121 would freeze the obligations of those statutes — the parts that bind developers *before* a model ships — while the federal rules replacing them sunset on the same three-year clock. The carve-outs for post-deployment activity, laws of general applicability, and common-law claims will not rescue frontier-safety statutes whose duties attach upstream. Congress would be asking the states to stand down for three years in exchange for a floor that expires with the ceiling.

This is also the opposite of what the country just decided. States enacted roughly 150 AI laws in 2026 alone, across 36 states. In July 2025 the Senate voted 99–1 to strip a proposed ten-year freeze on state AI laws out of the budget reconciliation bill. And our own August 2026 national survey (n = 1,512 registered voters; margin of error ±2.5 points) found 63% of voters say federal law should **not** block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

If Congress wants a single national rule, it should be a national rule that stops the race — a floor states may build on, not a ceiling they must live under.

## 4. What we ask you to write instead

**One: pause.** An immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 FLOP, in force until Congress certifies — on the basis of independent testing reported by CAISI — that such systems can be reliably controlled. We would suggest a public report followed by a certification vote, so that the decision to resume is a decision someone stands behind.

**Two: wind down.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM — and it means U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. We know this is the hardest ask in this letter. It is also the one our members care most about. Once weights are public, anyone can run them, and no later rule can recall them.

**Three: personal accountability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation. Sixty-six percent of voters in our survey support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. A $1 million-per-day civil fine against a company that has lost control of a frontier model's weights is not a deterrent; it is a line item.

**Four: keep the states armed.** Strike Section 121. Our moratorium is designed as a federal floor; states should remain free to go further.

**Five: CAISI, but as enforcement.** We support codifying CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium: certification testing, monitoring of large training runs, verifying the wind-down, and referring knowing violations to the Department of Justice. The draft's $100 million per year for FY2027–2029 is a start, not a substitute, and fee authority drawn from the developers CAISI oversees should not stand in for appropriations.

## 5. Where we can work with you

We support Section 113's anti-retaliation protections for employees and contractors who report AI violations, which is consistent with the whistleblower protections we asked for in our March 2025 comment to OSTP on the AI Action Plan. Keep them, strengthen them, and make sure they travel with the rest of the framework. We also welcome the draft's attention to model-weight security and to the open-source ecosystem.

## 6. A word on where this is going

We understand the frontier title has since been introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925 (July 23, 2026), referred to Energy and Commerce and to Science, Space and Technology. Our comments apply to it in full. Three things in the introduced text concern us, and we flag them because we would rather be corrected than imprecise: the covered class appears to narrow to "very large frontier developers" — more than $5 billion in gross revenue plus $10 billion in AI-related development expenditures over 36 months; the catastrophic-risk trigger adds a "single incident" limitation; and Section 9's preemption does not appear to carry the three-year sunset that Section 121 had, nor the whistleblower protections of Section 113.

## 7. The politics, briefly

Our August 2026 survey found 74% of voters agree Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 52% are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, with 31% opposed. On the substance, the industry's own voices are moving our way: in June 2026, Anthropic said publicly that frontier developers should establish a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier development, and warned about the risk of humans losing control of AI systems. When a frontier developer says the world should have the option to pause, and the congressional response is a 15-day reporting form, the gap between the risk and the response is the whole story. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

We would welcome a meeting with you or your staff before introduction or markup, and we can bring members from your districts who want to be heard on this. Please contact me at [EMAIL] or [PHONE]. Thank you for taking the draft out for comment, and for taking this one seriously.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[STREET ADDRESS, CITY, STATE ZIP]
[EMAIL] | [PHONE]

*Enclosures: FRC national survey toplines (August 2026); FRC asks by section; FRC comment to OSTP, AI Action Plan RFI (March 14, 2025).*

*Sources relied on for facts in this letter: sponsors' discussion draft and section-by-section summary (June 4, 2026); Roll Call, June 4, 2026; DLA Piper, June 5, 2026; Future Privacy Forum, June 9, 2026; Epoch AI trends and model-threshold analyses (Feb. 2026); Reuters, June 4, 2026 (Anthropic); congress.gov, H.R. 9925; Governor's Office, State of California (SB 53 signing, Sept. 29, 2025); NY DFS press release (RAISE Act).*"}

# FRC comment letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)

> **INTERNAL DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off, Fri 23 Oct 2026.** Do not transmit from this workspace. Delete this note block and fill every [BRACKETED] item before sending. Section numbers are keyed to the sponsors' June 4, 2026 discussion draft; the postscript flags what changed in the introduced text (H.R. 9925) and what still needs confirmation.

---

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We write to respond to your invitation for comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft.

Our bottom line is simple, and we want to state it plainly at the top: **we oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium** — a pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP (a standard measure of the computing power used to train a model) until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.

We say this after reading the draft, and after two years of hearing from our members. Parents ask us who is accountable if a frontier model is stolen. Warehouse and hospital workers ask what happens to the systems that increasingly schedule them. Our researchers cannot point us to a single developer who can demonstrate control of its most capable system. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

We are grateful that you released this as a discussion draft and invited feedback before introduction. That process is why we are engaging rather than merely objecting. Our comments follow.

## 1. The draft measures the race; it does not slow it

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of the model weights of a frontier model; a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and loss of control of a model. Those are exactly the events that no reporting regime can undo. Once weights are out, they are out.

Section 111 responds to that reality with disclosure. Large frontier developers must publish a "frontier AI framework" describing how they assess and manage catastrophic risk. All frontier developers must publish transparency reports before or alongside deployment, and must report critical safety incidents to the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) — within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours for imminent catastrophic risk.

Section 112 responds with an audit. Large frontier developers must retain a CAISI-licensed Independent Verification Organization to verify compliance and assess the adequacy of their frameworks, semi-annually and on request.

We support transparency. We support audits. But read together, these are the parts of a safety regime that operate *after* the hardest decisions have already been made. No provision in the draft asks anyone to stop, and no official in the draft has the power to make them. An IVO can refer a violation to the Attorney General, and must refer matters involving imminent catastrophic risk — but referral is not suspension, and an audit delivered six months into a deployment is not a gate. The principal sanction, civil penalties of up to $1 million per day, prices non-compliance for companies spending billions on training runs.

There is also the sunset. Sections 111 and 112 expire after three years unless Congress reauthorizes them. A safety regime that expires on a schedule is a pilot program, not a floor.

## 2. The thresholds in Section 101 pick a perimeter that decays

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, and tiers developers by revenue ($50 million for a "frontier developer," $500 million for a "large frontier developer").

We agree that 10^26 is the right line. It is the same line our moratorium proposal uses. But as a regulatory perimeter it decays quickly. Training compute for frontier language models has grown roughly five-fold per year since 2020. The first model estimated to cross 10^26 FLOP was Grok-3, released in February 2025; on current trend, around 30 notable models will sit above that threshold by the start of 2027, and over 200 by 2030 (Epoch AI, Feb. 2026). What is "frontier" in this draft will be unremarkable by 2028, and the bill's obligations will follow the frontier upward rather than holding it.

The revenue tiers leave out actors our members worry about most: labs under the revenue line, non-profit and university efforts, and foreign or state-backed developers whose models matter regardless of what they earn. And the definition of catastrophic risk — death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage — is pegged to identifiable catastrophes. Our members worry as much about slow, cumulative harms: gradual loss of human oversight, misuse that never crosses the 50-person line, and models that quietly become harder to inspect. Those harms fall outside the draft's frame entirely.

## 3. Section 121 would disarm the states. We oppose it.

Section 121 preempts state law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years, and "development" reaches every act a developer pe
... [416 chars truncated] ...
 the obligations of those statutes — the parts that bind developers *before* a model ships — while the federal rules replacing them sunset on the same three-year clock. The carve-outs for post-deployment activity, laws of general applicability, and common-law claims will not rescue frontier-safety statutes whose duties attach upstream. Congress would be asking the states to stand down for three years in exchange for a floor that expires with the ceiling.

This is also the opposite of what the country just decided. States enacted roughly 150 AI laws in 2026 alone, across 36 states. In July 2025 the Senate voted 99–1 to strip a proposed ten-year freeze on state AI laws out of the budget reconciliation bill. And our own August 2026 national survey (n = 1,512 registered voters; margin of error ±2.5 points) found 63% of voters say federal law should **not** block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

If Congress wants a single national rule, it should be a national rule that stops the race — a floor states may build on, not a ceiling they must live under.

## 4. What we ask you to write instead

**One: pause.** An immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 FLOP, in force until Congress certifies — on the basis of independent testing reported by CAISI — that such systems can be reliably controlled. We would suggest a public report followed by a certification vote, so that the decision to resume is a decision someone stands behind.

**Two: wind down.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM — and it means U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. We know this is the hardest ask in this letter. It is also the one our members care most about. Once weights are public, anyone can run them, and no later rule can recall them.

**Three: personal accountability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation. Sixty-six percent of voters in our survey support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. A $1 million-per-day civil fine against a company that has lost control of a frontier model's weights is not a deterrent; it is a line item.

**Four: keep the states armed.** Strike Section 121. Our moratorium is designed as a federal floor; states should remain free to go further.

**Five: CAISI, but as enforcement.** We support codifying CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium: certification testing, monitoring of large training runs, verifying the wind-down, and referring knowing violations to the Department of Justice. The draft's $100 million per year for FY2027–2029 is a start, not a substitute, and fee authority drawn from the developers CAISI oversees should not stand in for appropriations.

## 5. Where we can work with you

We support Section 113's anti-retaliation protections for employees and contractors who report AI violations, which is consistent with the whistleblower protections we asked for in our March 2025 comment to OSTP on the AI Action Plan. Keep them, strengthen them, and make sure they travel with the rest of the framework. We also welcome the draft's attention to model-weight security and to the open-source ecosystem.

## 6. A word on where this is going

We understand the frontier title has since been introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925 (July 23, 2026), referred to Energy and Commerce and to Science, Space and Technology. Our comments apply to it in full. Three things in the introduced text concern us, and we flag them because we would rather be corrected than imprecise: the covered class appears to narrow to "very large frontier developers" — more than $5 billion in gross revenue plus $10 billion in AI-related development expenditures over 36 months; the catastrophic-risk trigger adds a "single incident" limitation; and Section 9's preemption does not appear to carry the three-year sunset that Section 121 had, nor the whistleblower protections of Section 113.

## 7. The politics, briefly

Our August 2026 survey found 74% of voters agree Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 52% are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, with 31% opposed. On the substance, the industry's own voices are moving our way: in June 2026, Anthropic said publicly that frontier developers should establish a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier development, and warned about the risk of humans losing control of AI systems. When a frontier developer says the world should have the option to pause, and the congressional response is a 15-day reporting form, the gap between the risk and the response is the whole story. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

We would welcome a meeting with you or your staff before introduction or markup, and we can bring members from your districts who want to be heard on this. Please contact me at [EMAIL] or [PHONE]. Thank you for taking the draft out for comment, and for taking this one seriously.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[STREET ADDRESS, CITY, STATE ZIP]
[EMAIL] | [PHONE]

*Enclosures: FRC national survey toplines (August 2026); FRC asks by section; FRC comment to OSTP, AI Action Plan RFI (March 14, 2025).*

*Sources relied on for facts in this letter: sponsors' discussion draft and section-by-section summary (June 4, 2026); Roll Call, June 4, 2026; DLA Piper, June 5, 2026; Future Privacy Forum, June 9, 2026; Epoch AI trends and model-threshold analyses (Feb. 2026); Reuters, June 4, 2026 (Anthropic); congress.gov, H.R. 9925; Governor's Office, State of California (SB 53 signing, Sept. 29, 2025); NY DFS press release (RAISE Act).*

# FRC comment letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)

> **INTERNAL DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off, Fri 23 Oct 2026.** Do not transmit from this workspace. Delete this note block and fill every [BRACKETED] item before sending. Section numbers are keyed to the sponsors' June 4, 2026 discussion draft; Section 6 flags what changed in the introduced text (H.R. 9925) and what still needs confirmation.

---

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a 501(c)(4) coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We write to respond to your invitation for comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft.

Our bottom line is simple, and we want to state it plainly at the top: **we oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace its frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium** — a pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP (a standard measure of the computing power used to train a model) until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.

We say this after reading the draft, and after listening to our members. Parents ask us who is accountable if a frontier model is stolen. Warehouse and hospital workers ask what happens to the systems that increasingly schedule them. Our researchers cannot point us to a single developer who can demonstrate control of its most capable system. Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

We are grateful that you released this as a discussion draft and invited feedback before introduction. That process is why we are engaging rather than merely objecting. Our comments follow.

## 1. The draft measures the race; it does not slow it

Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of the model weights of a frontier model; a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures; and loss of control of a model. Those are exactly the events that no reporting regime can undo. Once weights are out, they are out.

Section 111 responds to that reality with disclosure. Large frontier developers must publish a "frontier AI framework" describing how they assess and manage catastrophic risk. All frontier developers must publish transparency reports before or alongside deployment, and must report critical safety incidents to the Director of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) — within 15 days of discovery, or within 24 hours for imminent catastrophic risk.

Section 112 responds with an audit. Large frontier developers must retain a CAISI-licensed Independent Verification Organization to verify compliance and assess the adequacy of their frameworks, semi-annually and on request.

We support transparency. We support audits. But read together, these are the parts of a safety regime that operate *after* the hardest decisions have already been made. No provision in the draft asks anyone to stop, and no official in the draft has the power to make them. An IVO can refer a violation to the Attorney General, and must refer matters involving imminent catastrophic risk — but referral is not suspension, and an audit delivered six months into a deployment is not a gate. The principal sanction, civil penalties of up to $1 million per day, prices non-compliance for companies spending billions on training runs.

There is also the sunset. Sections 111 and 112 expire after three years unless Congress reauthorizes them. A safety regime that expires on a schedule is a pilot program, not a floor.

## 2. The thresholds in Section 101 pick a perimeter that decays

Section 101 defines a frontier model as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations, and tiers developers by revenue ($50 million for a "frontier developer," $500 million for a "large frontier developer").

We agree that 10^26 is the right line. It is the same line our moratorium proposal uses. But as a regulatory perimeter it decays quickly. Training compute for frontier language models has grown roughly five-fold per year since 2020. The first model estimated to cross 10^26 FLOP was Grok-3, released in February 2025; on current trend, around 30 notable models will sit above that threshold by the start of 2027, and over 200 by 2030 (Epoch AI, Feb. 2026). What is "frontier" in this draft will be unremarkable by 2028, and the bill's obligations will follow the frontier upward rather than holding it.

The revenue tiers leave out actors our members worry about most: labs under the revenue line, non-profit and university efforts, and foreign or state-backed developers whose models matter regardless of what they earn. And the definition of catastrophic risk — death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage — is pegged to identifiable catastrophes. Our members worry as much about slow, cumulative harms: gradual loss of human oversight, misuse that never crosses the 50-person line, and models that quietly become harder to inspect. Those harms fall outside the draft's frame entirely.

## 3. Section 121 would disarm the states. We oppose it.

Section 121 preempts state law "specifically regulating the development" of an AI model for three years, and "development" reaches every act a developer performs or directs before deployment. Your own FAQ concedes that California's AB 2013 and part of SB 942 would be preempted, and that the frontier safety laws — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois's SB 315 — would be "federalized."

Consider what that means in practice. SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect January 1, 2027. Section 121 would freeze the obligations of those statutes — the parts that bind developers *before* a model ships — while the federal rules replacing them sunset on the same three-year clock. The carve-outs for post-deployment activity, laws of general applicability, and common-law claims will not rescue frontier-safety statutes whose duties attach upstream. Congress would be asking the states to stand down for three years in exchange for a floor that expires with the ceiling.

This is also the opposite of what the country just decided. States enacted roughly 150 AI laws in 2026 alone, across 36 states. In July 2025 the Senate voted 99–1 to strip a proposed ten-year freeze on state AI laws out of the budget reconciliation bill. And our own August 2026 national survey (n = 1,512 registered voters; margin of error ±2.5 points) found 63% of voters say federal law should **not** block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

If Congress wants a single national rule, it should be a national rule that stops the race — a floor states may build on, not a ceiling they must live under.

## 4. What we ask you to write instead

**One: pause.** An immediate moratorium on training any model above 10^26 FLOP, in force until Congress certifies — on the basis of independent testing reported by CAISI — that such systems can be reliably controlled. We would suggest a public report followed by a certification vote, so that the decision to resume is a decision someone stands behind.

**Two: wind down.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM — and it means U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. We know this is the hardest ask in this letter. It is also the one our members care most about. Once weights are public, anyone can run them, and no later rule can recall them.

**Three: personal accountability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation. Sixty-six percent of voters in our survey support criminal penalties when AI systems cause mass harm. A $1 million-per-day civil fine against a company that has lost control of a frontier model's weights is not a deterrent; it is a line item.

**Four: keep the states armed.** Strike Section 121. Our moratorium is designed as a federal floor; states should remain free to go further.

**Five: CAISI, but as enforcement.** We support codifying CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium: certification testing, monitoring of large training runs, verifying the wind-down, and referring knowing violations to the Department of Justice. The draft's $100 million per year for FY2027–2029 is a start, not a substitute, and fee authority drawn from the developers CAISI oversees should not stand in for appropriations.

## 5. Where we can work with you

We support Section 113's anti-retaliation protections for employees and contractors who report AI violations, which is consistent with the whistleblower protections we asked for in our March 2025 comment to OSTP on the AI Action Plan. Keep them, strengthen them, and make sure they travel with the rest of the framework. We also welcome the draft's attention to model-weight security and to the open-source ecosystem.

## 6. A word on where this is going

We understand the frontier title has since been introduced as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925 (July 23, 2026), referred to Energy and Commerce and to Science, Space and Technology. Our comments apply to it in full. Three things in the introduced text concern us, and we flag them because we would rather be corrected than imprecise: the covered class appears to narrow to "very large frontier developers" — more than $5 billion in gross revenue plus $10 billion in AI-related development expenditures over 36 months; the catastrophic-risk trigger adds a "single incident" limitation; and Section 9's preemption does not appear to carry the three-year sunset that Section 121 had, nor the whistleblower protections of Section 113.

## 7. The politics, briefly

Our August 2026 survey found 74% of voters agree Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; 52% are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; and 49% support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, with 31% opposed. On the substance, the industry's own voices are moving our way: in June 2026, Anthropic said publicly that frontier developers should establish a coordinated, verifiable way to slow or temporarily pause frontier development, and warned about the risk of humans losing control of AI systems. When a frontier developer says the world should have the option to pause, and the congressional response is a 15-day reporting form, the gap between the risk and the response is the whole story. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

We would welcome a meeting with you or your staff before introduction or markup, and we can bring members from your districts who want to be heard on this. Please contact me at [EMAIL] or [PHONE]. Thank you for taking the draft out for comment, and for taking this one seriously.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
[STREET ADDRESS, CITY, STATE ZIP]
[EMAIL] | [PHONE]

*Enclosures: FRC national survey toplines (August 2026); FRC asks by section; FRC comment to OSTP, AI Action Plan RFI (March 14, 2025).*

*Sources relied on for facts in this letter: sponsors' discussion draft and section-by-section summary (June 4, 2026); Roll Call, June 4, 2026; DLA Piper, June 5, 2026; Future Privacy Forum, June 9, 2026; Epoch AI trends and model-threshold analyses (Feb. 2026); Reuters, June 4, 2026 (Anthropic); congress.gov, H.R. 9925; Governor's Office, State of California (SB 53 signing, Sept. 29, 2025); NY DFS press release (RAISE Act).*

# FRC staff Q&A — anticipated questions

*Staff draft for Executive Director sign-off, Fri 23 Oct 2026. Answers verified at ≤120 words each. Use with the one-pager and the asks-by-section table.*

**Q1 (Majority E&C staff): "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"**

Because both act after the fact. The draft's own definition of a critical safety incident — exfiltrated weights, failed risk mitigation, loss of control — describes events a report cannot undo. CAISI's guidelines are voluntary. IVO audits are semi-annual, paid by the audited developer, and cannot stop a release; they refer violations rather than suspend them. Sections 111 and 112 even sunset after three years. No one can show these systems are controllable, and training compute grows roughly five-fold a year. Reporting measures the race. Nothing in the draft pauses it. That is the gap our comment letter is about.

**Q2 (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned): "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"**

Dropping preemption entirely is necessary but not sufficient. Shortened, it is worse than it sounds: Section 121 would freeze state frontier-safety laws for the window while Sections 111 and 112 sunset on the same three-year clock — the federal floor expires with the state ceiling. California's SB 53 is already in force; New York's RAISE Act starts January 1, 2027. Remove Section 121 and we will engage in good faith, but our board position stands: replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a moratorium. And 63% of voters say federal law should not block state AI laws; the Senate voted 99–1 in July 2025 to strip a ten-year freeze.

**Q3 (Senate Commerce staff): "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"**

The race is the risk, not the shield. A pause costs us only if a rival can safely build what we will not — and no one, American or Chinese, can show that. Large training runs are also hard to hide: they need gigawatt-scale power and export-controlled accelerators, which makes a pause verifiable and gives the United States real leverage to negotiate a multilateral pause. Meanwhile U.S.-led open-weight releases — Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM — already hand frontier capability to anyone, including adversaries. Slowing down is how we set the verification standard the world follows. Even Anthropic, a frontier developer, said in June 2026 the world should have the option to pause.

**Q4 (Appropriations staff): "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"**

Honestly: $100 million a year is modest for the job, but our objection is the mandate, not the money. As drafted CAISI writes voluntary guidelines, evaluates systems and licenses auditors — that is monitoring, not enforcement. We support CAISI as the enforcement body for a moratorium: running certification testing, watching large training runs, verifying the wind-down of uncertifiable models, and referring knowing violations to the Justice Department.
